name: Silicon solar array
blurb: Cheap, proven panels. Heavy for the power they make, and weak far from the Sun.
notes: Power generation and storage are modeled as mission-scale subsystems.

name: Triple-junction solar array
blurb: High-efficiency gallium-arsenide cells: almost twice the power per square metre.
heritage: Multi-junction solar arrays, as flown on Juno
notes: Juno demonstrates solar power at Jupiter. Cell efficiency at 1 AU and assembled array mass and degradation are catalog estimates.

name: Radioisotope generator (MMRTG)
blurb: Plutonium-238 heat turned into ~110 W, day and night, anywhere. Expensive and scarce.
notes: The NASA/DOE fact sheet reports about 110 W at mission start and 45 kg. Cost, failure rate and the constant annual power decline are game assumptions.

name: Li-ion battery, 200 Wh
blurb: Enough for a small spacecraft through a short eclipse.
notes: The capacity is the nominal game pack size. Pack mass and depth-of-discharge limit are estimates.

name: Li-ion battery, 500 Wh
blurb: A mid-size pack for low-orbit eclipses.
notes: The capacity is the nominal game pack size. Pack mass and depth-of-discharge limit are estimates.

name: Li-ion battery, 1.5 kWh
blurb: Big enough to keep a large orbiter alive through long shadows.
notes: The capacity is the nominal game pack size. Pack mass and depth-of-discharge limit are estimates.

name: Li-ion battery, 4 kWh
blurb: Flagship-class energy storage.
notes: The capacity is the nominal game pack size. Pack mass and depth-of-discharge limit are estimates.

name: Hydrazine monopropellant
blurb: Simple and reliable, but inefficient — fine for small burns, painful for big ones.
notes: Mass, draw and tank fraction represent a modeled propulsion assembly.

name: Bipropellant main engine
blurb: Fuel + oxidiser for a powerful, efficient engine. The standard for orbit insertion.
notes: Juno’s Leros-1b engine is rated at 645 N. The catalog estimates the mass and power of the full installation, its specific impulse and its tank fraction.

name: Ion engine (solar electric)
blurb: Uses propellant efficiently but accelerates slowly. Needs plenty of electrical power and cannot brake quickly into a planetary orbit.
heritage: Xenon ion propulsion, as flown on Dawn
notes: Dawn is the flight precedent for xenon ion propulsion. The listed numbers model a larger electric propulsion package. It draws operating power while thrusting.

name: Low-gain antenna only
blurb: Talks from almost any orientation, but whispers. Fine at the Moon, hopeless at Jupiter.
notes: The mass and aperture efficiency are modeled. The DSN handbook describes the link equations and the receiving stations.

name: High-gain dish, 0.5 m
blurb: A small dish for nearby targets.
notes: The mass and aperture efficiency are modeled. The DSN handbook describes the link equations and the receiving stations.

name: High-gain dish, 1.5 m
blurb: A solid all-rounder for Mars.
notes: The mass and aperture efficiency are modeled. The DSN handbook describes the link equations and the receiving stations.

name: High-gain dish, 2.5 m
blurb: Outer-planet class. Juno carries one this size.
notes: JPL DESCANSO Section 2.1.4.1 specifies a 2.5 m dual-band high-gain antenna on Juno. Mass and aperture efficiency are modeled.

name: High-gain dish, 3.0 m
blurb: A Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter-sized dish. More gain makes it easier to send back large files.
notes: JPL DESCANSO Section 2.1.4.1 gives MRO’s high-gain dish diameter as 3 m. The mass and aperture efficiency are modeled. The DSN handbook describes the link equations and the receiving stations.

name: Deployable mesh dish, 5 m
blurb: Unfolds like an umbrella for huge gain at low mass. If it doesn't open, you're in trouble.
heritage: Galileo's umbrella antenna (which famously failed to open)
notes: The mass and aperture efficiency are modeled. The DSN handbook describes the link equations and the receiving stations. Galileo pioneered the umbrella-style deployment and experienced a partial deployment. The game models a generic 5 m dish.

name: 5 W solid-state amplifier
blurb: Tiny and frugal.
notes: The rated RF power is the modeled output. Electrical draw follows the assumed amplifier efficiency.

name: 20 W solid-state amplifier
blurb: A dependable mid-power radio.
notes: The rated RF power is the modeled output. Electrical draw follows the assumed amplifier efficiency.

name: 35 W travelling-wave tube
blurb: Efficient high-power amplifier for deep space.
notes: The rated RF power is the modeled output. Electrical draw follows the assumed amplifier efficiency.

name: 100 W travelling-wave tube
blurb: High-output radio amplifier. Useful for large data returns if your power system can support it.
notes: The rated RF power is the modeled output. Electrical draw follows the assumed amplifier efficiency.

name: Coarse pointing (sun sensors + thrusters)
blurb: Keeps you roughly aimed. Not good enough for big dishes or telescopes.
notes: Pointing accuracy, power and mass represent a generic control system.

name: Star trackers + reaction wheels
blurb: Star trackers tell you where you are pointing. Reaction wheels turn the spacecraft without using propellant.
heritage: Star trackers and reaction wheels are common attitude-control components
notes: Pointing accuracy, power and mass represent a generic control system.

name: Precision pointing suite
blurb: Dual star trackers, gyros and wheels — rock-steady aim for telescopes and Ka-band.
notes: Pointing accuracy, power and mass represent a generic control system.

name: Commercial-grade flight computer
blurb: Fast and cheap, from the small-satellite world. Radiation is its enemy.
notes: The estimates cover a flight computer and onboard recorder. Radiation tolerance varies with the parts and shielding.

name: Radiation-tolerant computer
blurb: The deep-space standard (RAD750-class) with a 160 Gb recorder.
notes: The Juno spacecraft press kit verifies RAD750 flight heritage. The 160 Gb recorder represents the modeled package.

name: Radiation-hardened computer + big recorder
blurb: Shrugs off harsh radiation and stores a terabit of data.
notes: The estimates cover a flight computer and onboard recorder. Radiation tolerance varies with the parts and shielding.

name: Passive thermal (blankets + radiators)
blurb: Blankets and radiators need little power, but the spacecraft can get too cold far from the Sun.
notes: Mass, electrical load and heater demand approximate a thermal-control package.

name: Active thermal (heaters + louvres)
blurb: Electric heaters keep you warm anywhere — at a power cost that grows with distance.
notes: Mass, electrical load and heater demand approximate a thermal-control package. heaterWPerAU is a game-balance value, tuned so the Juno-like reference design lands inside its 10–40% power margin target at Jupiter.

name: Radioisotope heater units
blurb: Tiny plutonium pellets give free warmth for decades. Large missions only.
notes: Mass, electrical load and heater demand approximate a thermal-control package.

name: No extra shielding
blurb: Electronics rely on the spacecraft's own structure.
notes: The dose factor is a game modeling assumption and depends on the shielding geometry and environment in a real mission.

name: Spot shielding
blurb: Local shielding protects vulnerable electronics. The game models a 50% dose reduction.
notes: The dose factor is a game modeling assumption and depends on the shielding geometry and environment in a real mission.

name: Titanium radiation vault
blurb: A thick-walled box for all the electronics. Heavy, but it's how Juno survives Jupiter.
notes: Mass verified: NSSDCA 2011-040A gives Juno's titanium vault as 150 kg with walls over 1 cm thick. doseFactor and cost are game values. The dose factor is a game modeling assumption and depends on the shielding geometry and environment in a real mission.
